newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan insurers finalise rescue plan for Nissan Life.
newsitem.headline: Japan insurers finalise rescue plan for Nissan Life.

text.p: Japan's life insurance industry announced on Friday that it had hammered out a framework to deal with huge losses at failed Nissan Mutual Life Insurance.

The scheme, which calls on policyholders to accept a cut in guaranteed returns on their policies, was finalised two months after the Ministry of Finance (MOF) suspended Nissan Life from business on April 25.
It marked the first failure of a life insurance firm in post-war Japan.
Makoto Fukuda, director of MOF's insurance department, said on Friday that the ministry does not think other life insurance firms will fail like Nissan Life.
"I don't think what has happened to Nissan Life will happen again. I cannot see behavior in other firms such as was shown in Nissan Life. There are no such firms," he told reporters.
The insurer suffered heavy losses through excessive stock and real estate investments in the late 1980s "bubble era" of inflated asset prices.

Nearly half of Nissan Life's assets consist of pension fund contracts held by individuals that guarantee a high return of about 5.5 percent. Those commitments also damaged the company's financial stability.
Nissan Life's actual liabilities exceeded its assets by around 300 billion yen ($2.63 billion), larger than an earlier estimate of 200 billion yen ($1.75 billion).

But analysts said that the collapse of Nissan Life has made customers more selective in choosing life insurance companies, which in turn may make it difficult for other financially weak insurers to stay afloat.

"Unless those weaker life insurers take measures to keep their customers confident, they may face difficulties in maintaining premium revenues," said Kouya Hasegawa, an analyst at Nikko Research Centre.

Under the framework adopted at a board meeting of the Life Insurance Association of Japan, the industry will set up a new company to liquidate Nissan Life by taking over its policies and managing them until they mature, the association said.
The association has been serving as an interim caretaker for Nissan Life since it went under.
Nissan Life is expected to obtain approval of the scheme from a policyholders' general meeting at the end of July.
The new company will cut the guaranteed rate of return to 2.75 percent in order to try to ensure profitability.

The Policyholders Protection Fund, comprised of contributions from life insurers, will inject 200 billion yen ($1.75 billion) into the new company, and the remaining 100 billion yen ($877 million) in the debts will be covered over the next five years through the company's profits.

To ensure premium revenue, the new company will discourage policyholders from cancelling their contracts by cutting refunds by a maximum 15 percent, and no dividends will be paid to policyholders until the new company covers the remaining 100 billion yen ($877 million) in losses, the association said.

Association chairman Kenjiro Hata told reporters that the industry body would continue to ask Hitachi Ltd and Nissan Motor Co Ltd for support for the scheme by hiring Nissan Life employees and by refraining from cancelling policies they hold with the insurer.

Hitachi and Nissan Motor, Nissan Life's two largest clients, have rejected the association's requests to assist in the restructuring, which forced the association to draw up the scheme to liquidate the life insurer. ($1=114 yen)
